analogy.p: Imagine a family whose money is held in several accounts (your energy stores) inside a sealed vault (a closed system). Moving money between accounts never changes the total in the vault, just like energy shifting between stores. If the vault has a leak and coins roll out into the street (dissipation), the money is not destroyed but it is now spread out and very hard to collect back. The analogy breaks down because energy has no single 'currency' and, unlike money, you can never make more of it by printing.

bullets: **Energy cannot be created or destroyed**, only transferred from one store to another or dissipated (spread out) into the surroundings.
The **total energy** before an event equals the **total energy** after it, provided you count every store, including the thermal store of the surroundings.
Energy is measured in **joules (J)**; 1 kJ = 1000 J and 1 MJ = 1 000 000 J.
Energy can be **transferred usefully** (e.g. electrical energy to light in a lamp), **stored** (e.g. in a stretched spring) or **dissipated** (e.g. spread to the air as heat).
The law applies to **every** process in the specification: mechanical, electrical, thermal, chemical and nuclear.
A statement such as 'the energy was used up' is **wrong**: energy is not used up, it is transferred to a less useful store.
core.h: The law of conservation of energy
core.p: The **principle of conservation of energy** states that **energy can be transferred usefully, stored or dissipated, but cannot be created or destroyed**. This is one of the most important ideas in all of physics. It means that whenever something happens (a ball falls, a kettle boils, a car brakes) the energy does not vanish: it moves from one store to another or spreads out into the surroundings. If a question seems to show energy 'disappearing', the correct response is always to ask where it has gone.

bullets: A system can be a **single object** (a moving car), **two objects** (a ball and the Earth) or a **group** (a kettle, the water and the air round it).
The **energy stores** are: kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, thermal, chemical, magnetic, electrostatic and nuclear.

Energy is transferred between stores in four ways: **mechanically** (a force moving through a distance), **electrically** (a current), **by heating** (conduction, convection, radiation) and **by radiation** (light or sound waves).
Always state the system you are considering: it makes your answer to 'where does the energy go?' precise.
Changes in energy stores are described as **energy transfers** (e.g. 'chemical to kinetic') and you should name both stores and the way energy is transferred.
If you include the surroundings in the system, then no energy leaves the system, which leads to the idea of a closed system.
core.p: A **system** is an **object or a group of objects** that you choose to look at. When a system changes, energy is transferred between its parts, so the way energy is shared out between the **energy stores** changes. Choosing the system is a modelling decision: you draw an imaginary boundary around the objects you care about and then account for energy crossing that boundary. For example, if you study a ball falling to the ground, the system could be the ball and the Earth together, because the gravitational potential store belongs to the pair of objects.

bullets: Definition: a closed system is one where there are **no net changes in the total energy** as the system changes (AQA: 'a closed system is a system in which neither energy nor matter can enter or leave').
Inside a closed system energy can be **transferred between stores** (e.g. gravitational potential to kinetic and thermal), but the **total stays the same**.
The **sum of all the energy changes** in a closed system is **zero**: gains in some stores are exactly balanced by losses from others.
A perfectly closed system is an **idealisation**: in real life energy leaks to the surroundings, so we include the surroundings to make the system closed.
Example: a thermos flask containing hot tea is nearly closed, so the tea cools very slowly.
An **open system** can exchange energy (and often matter) with its surroundings, such as an uncovered cup of tea losing steam and heat.
core.p: A **closed system** is a system in which **neither matter nor energy can enter or leave**; there are no **net** energy transfers into or out of the system. Because nothing crosses the boundary, the **total energy of a closed system is constant**. Energy can still be shuffled between the stores inside the system, so the **net change in the total energy is zero**. The Universe is the biggest closed system, but in practice we treat a suitably large system, including the surroundings, as closed.

bullets: Gravitational potential energy: **Ep = m g h** (J), with m in kg, g = 9.8 N/kg and h in m.
Kinetic energy: **Ek = ½ m v²** (J), with m in kg and v in m/s.
With **no friction or air resistance**: **loss in Ep = gain in Ek**, so m g h = ½ m v².
Cancel m: **v² = 2 g h**, so **v = √(2 g h)**; the speed does not depend on the mass.
With resistive forces: **loss in Ep = gain in Ek + energy dissipated as heat**, so v is **smaller** than √(2 g h).
As the object falls its Ep falls linearly with height, but its Ek rises with the **square** of speed.
core.h: Energy transfers inside a closed system: the falling object
core.p: When an object falls with no resistive force, **gravitational potential energy** is transferred to **kinetic energy**, and the total stays constant. If there is **air resistance** or friction, some energy is dissipated to the **thermal store** of the object and the air. Counting the thermal store of the air as part of the system keeps the total constant. This is the model behind many exam calculations.

bullets: **Pendulum**: gravitational potential to kinetic and back; each swing is slightly lower because some energy is transferred to the **thermal store** of the air (air resistance) and the pivot (friction).

**Bouncing ball**: gravitational potential to kinetic to **elastic potential** (during contact) to kinetic to gravitational potential; the ball never returns to its start height because energy is dissipated as thermal energy and sound.
**Spring and mass**: elastic potential to kinetic to gravitational potential, with gradual loss to the thermal store.
**Car braking**: kinetic energy of the car is transferred mechanically by friction to the thermal energy of the brake discs and pads, then dissipated to the air.
**Electric kettle**: electrical energy is transferred to the thermal store of the water (useful) and to the surroundings (wasted).
**Roller coaster**: a motor does work to increase gravitational potential energy at the top, then Ep is transferred to Ek and to thermal energy by friction and air resistance.
core.h: Energy transfers in other everyday systems
core.p: The same principle explains energy changes in many familiar situations. In each case, identify the **initial store**, the **final stores** and the **useful** and **wasted** parts. Writing the full energy transfer chain is a regular 2 to 4 mark question, and examiners expect the thermal store of the surroundings to be mentioned whenever there is friction, resistance or sound.

bullets: **Dissipated** energy is energy that is spread out and stored in a less useful way, mostly as **thermal energy of the surroundings**.
Ways energy is wasted: **friction** between moving parts, **air resistance** (drag), **electrical resistance** in wires (heating), **sound** and **light** that are not wanted.
A device cannot make wasted energy useful again because the energy is spread across billions of particles in random motion.
The total energy input is always equal to the **useful energy output plus wasted energy output**.
**Input energy = useful output energy + wasted energy**: use this to find a missing value in a diagram.
The idea that energy becomes **less useful** as it dissipates connects to the choice of fuels, power stations and efficient design.
core.p: Energy that is **usefully transferred** is the energy that does the job the device was designed to do. Energy that is not useful is called **wasted energy**. Wasted energy is nearly always transferred to the **thermal store of the surroundings**, where it is **dissipated**: spread out among many particles so that it becomes very hard to use again. Dissipated energy is not destroyed; it is just no longer useful. This is why we say that energy is **conserved** but 'useful' energy is not.

bullets: The **input** arrow is on the left and splits into the **useful** output and the **wasted** outputs.
The widths are to scale: if the input is 100 J and the useful output is 40 J, the useful arrow is 40% of the width of the input arrow.
The sum of the outputs must equal the input: **100 J = 40 J + 60 J**.
To find a missing value, subtract the known outputs from the input.
Always include **units (J)** and label each arrow clearly.
Efficiency = useful output energy transfer ÷ total input energy transfer (covered in detail in the efficiency notes).
core.p: A **Sankey diagram** shows how the energy input to a device is split between useful and wasted outputs. The width of each arrow is drawn **in proportion to the amount of energy** it represents. The total width of the outputs must equal the width of the input, which is the principle of conservation of energy shown visually. You may also be given an energy flow diagram with numbers and asked to find an unknown value.

bullets: **Kinetic energy** = 0.5 × mass × speed²: Ek = ½ m v². Learn this; it is not given.
**Gravitational potential energy** = mass × gravitational field strength × height: Ep = m g h. Learn this; it is not given.
**Elastic potential energy** = 0.5 × spring constant × extension²: Ee = ½ k e² (provided the limit of proportionality is not exceeded).
**Change in thermal energy**: ΔE = m c Δθ, with c the specific heat capacity in J/kg°C.
Rearrangements: v = √(2 Ek ÷ m); h = Ep ÷ (m g); m = Ep ÷ (g h).
Check that **mass is in kg**, **height in m**, **speed in m/s** and **energy in J** before substituting.
core.h: Conservation of energy and mechanical calculations
core.p: Calculation questions are usually solved by writing an **energy balance**: the energy at the start equals the energy at the end, then rearranging for the unknown. Always state which stores are involved and write the equation in words first. You will be given g = 9.8 N/kg when needed, but check the question for the value used (some use 10 N/kg). Remember that the equations used here are on the AQA equation sheet only in part, so learn them.

bullets: **Step 1**: list the stores at the start (e.g. gravitational potential) and at the end (e.g. kinetic and thermal).
**Step 2**: write the energy equation in words: energy at start = energy at end.
**Step 3**: substitute numbers with correct units.
**Step 4**: rearrange to make the unknown the subject, then calculate and give a sensible number of significant figures.
**Step 5**: check units and whether the answer is realistic (a car at 400 m/s is not).
If energy is dissipated, the dissipated amount = **initial energy − final useful energy**.
core.h: Applying energy conservation: a worked method
core.p: A reliable method for any energy-conservation problem avoids mistakes. Identify the energy stores at the start and at the end, write an equation that equates the totals, include a term for dissipated energy if the question mentions friction or air resistance, and then substitute and rearrange. Check that your answer is sensible, for instance that a speed is not larger than the ideal speed if there is friction.

bullets: A **perpetual motion machine** that outputs more energy than it takes in would break the conservation of energy, so it is impossible.
Even in a vacuum a moving object would still have **friction in bearings** unless it has none, so some dissipation always happens.
We reduce dissipation by **lubrication**, **streamlining**, **insulation** and using **low-resistance** wires.
In an experiment, measured energy transfers are usually **smaller than predicted** because of dissipation, which is a common conclusion in evaluation questions.
The more energy is dissipated, the lower the **efficiency** of the device.
Idealisations (no air resistance) make calculations simple but give answers that are slightly too high for speed.
core.h: Real systems are never perfectly closed
core.p: In real life energy always leaks out of a system into the surroundings, so no practical system is completely closed. This is why perpetual motion machines cannot exist: any machine that keeps moving would need to avoid every dissipative process, which is impossible. It also explains why a bouncing ball eventually stops and why a swing needs pushing. Recognising the idealisations in a model (no friction, no air resistance) is a key evaluation skill in practical and data-handling questions.

bullets: **Forces and work done**: work done = force × distance moved along the line of action, and equals the energy transferred.
**Power**: power = energy transferred ÷ time (or work done ÷ time), in watts.
**Efficiency**: efficiency = useful output energy transfer ÷ total input energy transfer.
**Electricity**: E = P t and E = Q V describe energy transferred electrically; resistance causes dissipation as heat.
**Energy resources**: power stations transfer stored energy to electrical energy, always with some wasted as thermal.
**Waves and radiation**: waves transfer energy from a source to a receiver without transferring matter.
core.p: Conservation of energy underpins almost every other topic in the course. It links the forces and motion calculations to the thermal physics and electricity content, and is the reason many different questions can be answered by the same few equations. Making these links explicit helps with synoptic questions where you need to combine ideas.

bullets: Friction increases the **random kinetic energy** of particles in the surfaces, so the **temperature rises**.
The energy then spreads by conduction, convection and radiation to cooler surroundings: this is **dissipation**.
Energy that is spread among many particles is statistically unlikely to become concentrated again, so wasted energy is not recoverable.
The **specific heat capacity** equation ΔE = m c Δθ allows you to calculate the temperature rise caused by friction.
When an object falls through air, the work done against air resistance increases the thermal energy of the air and the object.
When stating that energy is conserved, mention that the **total** energy in the system plus surroundings is constant.
core.h: Higher tier thinking: explaining with the particle model
core.p: At Higher tier you should link energy dissipation to the behaviour of particles. When a surface rubs against another, the kinetic energy of the large object is transferred to the random kinetic energy of the particles in the surfaces, which increases their thermal energy. This random motion spreads to the surroundings by collisions, which is why the energy is dissipated and cannot be fully recovered. Explaining in this way gains the extended-response marks.

exam: **State/Give (1 mark)**: 'Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred between stores' scores the mark; add 'or dissipated' to be safe.

**Describe the energy transfers (2 to 3 marks)**: name the start store, the end stores and the way it is transferred, e.g. 'gravitational potential energy to kinetic energy and thermal energy of the surroundings'.
**Explain why not 100% (2 marks)**: 'some energy is dissipated/transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings by friction/air resistance'.
**Calculate (3 to 4 marks)**: write the equation, substitute, calculate, include the unit; marks are for each step even if the final answer is wrong.
**Closed system (2 marks)**: 'no net change in total energy / energy transferred between stores inside but total constant'.
**Sankey diagrams**: arrow widths to scale, input arrow = sum of output arrows, label with J.
**6 mark questions**: structure your answer as stores at the start, transfers in the middle, stores at the end, then mention dissipation and conservation.
**Use the exact phrases**: 'transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings', 'dissipated', 'total energy is conserved'.
**Data/graph questions**: if energy values are given in a table, check that the totals before and after match and explain any difference as dissipation.
**Command words**: 'state' = short fact; 'describe' = what happens; 'explain' = what happens and why; 'calculate' = numbers with units.

mistakes.r: Energy is never used up; it is transferred to other stores, mostly the thermal store of the surroundings (dissipated).
mistakes.w: Energy is used up or lost when a device is switched on.

mistakes.r: The total energy stays the same; the wasted energy is dissipated to the surroundings and is less useful.
mistakes.w: Energy is wasted so the total energy decreases.

mistakes.r: Energy is transferred between stores inside a closed system; only the total is constant.
mistakes.w: A closed system cannot have energy transfers.

mistakes.r: Say energy is transferred to the thermal store, or transferred by heating; 'heat' is not a store.
mistakes.w: Heat energy is a type of energy.

mistakes.r: Ignoring air resistance, m cancels in mgh = ½mv², so speed depends only on height.
mistakes.w: A heavier object falls faster so has more speed at the bottom.

mistakes.r: Ek = ½ × m × v²; only the speed is squared.
mistakes.w: Kinetic energy = m v² (forgetting the half) or (½ m v)².

mistakes.r: Convert to kg and m before using Ep = mgh or Ek = ½mv².
mistakes.w: Using mass in grams or height in cm.

mistakes.r: Some energy is dissipated as thermal energy and sound, so less is available as gravitational potential energy.
mistakes.w: The ball does not bounce back to the same height because energy is destroyed.

summary: You must know that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred between stores, stored or dissipated, and that in a closed system the total energy never changes. You apply this to everything from falling objects to devices with wasted energy, and use it to solve calculations and explain where energy goes. It is the single most-used idea in Paper 1 physics.

terms.d: Energy can be transferred usefully, stored or dissipated, but cannot be created or destroyed.
An object or a group of objects.
A system in which neither matter nor energy can enter or leave, so there is no net change in total energy.
A place where energy is held, such as kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, thermal, chemical, magnetic, electrostatic or nuclear.
The movement of energy from one store to another mechanically, electrically, by heating or by radiation.
Energy that is spread out among the surroundings, usually as thermal energy, and is no longer useful.
Energy that is not usefully transferred, mostly dissipated to the surroundings.
Energy that is transferred to the store or in the form wanted from a device.
The energy stored in an object because of its height in a gravitational field: Ep = m g h.
The energy stored in a moving object: Ek = ½ m v².
The unit of energy; one joule is the energy transferred when a force of 1 N moves an object 1 m.
A diagram in which the width of each arrow is proportional to the energy it represents.
A force that opposes motion between surfaces in contact and transfers energy to the thermal store.
The drag force opposing the motion of an object through air.

worked.ans: v = 19.8 m/s (about 20 m/s). The mass of 450 kg cancels.
worked.q: A roller coaster car of mass 450 kg starts from rest at the top of a 20 m hill. Ignoring friction and air resistance, calculate its speed at the bottom. Use g = 9.8 N/kg. (4 marks)
steps: Energy lost as gravitational potential = energy gained as kinetic: m g h = ½ m v².
Cancel the mass: v² = 2 g h = 2 × 9.8 × 20 = 392.

worked.q: A 0.20 kg ball is thrown vertically upwards at 15 m/s. Ignoring air resistance, calculate the maximum height. Use g = 9.8 N/kg. (4 marks)
steps: Initial kinetic energy = ½ m v² = 0.5 × 0.20 × 15² = 0.5 × 0.20 × 225 = 22.5 J.
At the top all of it is gravitational potential energy: Ep = m g h = 22.5 J.

worked.ans: Energy is conserved but not all of it returns to the ball as gravitational potential energy: some is dissipated as thermal energy of the ball, floor and surroundings (and sound), so less energy is available to lift the ball and it reaches a lower height.
worked.q: A ball is dropped from 1.5 m and bounces back to only 1.1 m. Explain, in terms of energy, why it does not bounce back to its original height. (3 marks)
steps: Start: ball has gravitational potential energy, which is transferred to kinetic energy as it falls.
On impact, kinetic energy is transferred to elastic potential energy briefly, then back to kinetic energy.
Some energy is dissipated to the thermal store of the ball and floor and to sound.
